comparison: Both evaluate model performance claims (C26-C28, C39-C41, C130) with UNCERTAIN ratings. OpenEval raises concerns about exceptionally high metrics (AUC 0.99, Brier 0.006) suggesting overfitting, while peer reviewers focus on validation methodology issues, specifically the enriched external validation cohort. Both identify the external validation bias as problematic but emphasize different aspects of the concern.

Both address external validation methodology (C31, C99). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN noting the enriched cohort may inflate sensitivity/PPV, while peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, explicitly challenging the validation approach as 'biased/overoptimistic.' Peer review is more critical, treating this as a fundamental flaw rather than uncertainty.

OpenEval's UNCERTAIN rating for performance metrics (C29-C30 on calibration) contrasts with peer reviewers' SUPPORTED rating. Peer reviewers accept calibration and clinical utility metrics without specific critique, while OpenEval questions the extraordinarily low Brier score (0.006) as unusual for clinical prediction.

Perfect agreement on study limitations (C90-C96). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval describes the limitations as 'honest and comprehensive,' while peer reviewers implicitly accept them, noting alignment with their own concerns about generalizability and temporal data issues.

Perfect agreement on need for prospective validation (C128-C129). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval calls this 'responsible,' while peer reviewers agree clinical utility is conditional pending further validation, with one noting 'If this model works as claimed, it will be useful.'

Both evaluate patient selection and cohort characteristics (C18-C21, C97-C98, C100-C101) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval praises 'comprehensive documentation' and 'appropriate' design, while peer reviewers acknowledge this as a 'large cohort' from 'real-world large-scale data,' treating sample size as a strength.

Both address demographic and clinical predictors (C32-C33, C134) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes SHAP analysis support from Figure 3, while peer reviewers accept these findings as credible contributions without specific challenge.

Both evaluate laboratory predictors (C34-C35, C61, C127) but differ in confidence. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on SHAP analysis, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN due to temporal ambiguity—features may have occurred before PSE onset, undermining causal interpretation.

Both address age and NIHSS findings (C43-C44) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval praises acknowledgment of literature contradictions, while peer reviewers accept these predictors as credible without challenge, treating identification of key predictors as valid contribution.

Both evaluate complications and brain regions (C22-C23, C131-C132). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to missing effect sizes, confidence intervals, and multiple testing correction concerns. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting these clinical associations without methodological critique.

Both address brain region findings (C58) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the reconciliation between univariate associations and LASSO exclusion is 'reasonable interpretation,' while peer reviewers accept the statistical methodology without critique.

Both evaluate comorbidity patterns (C50-C52) but with different emphasis. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, calling the TOAST classification explanation 'largely speculative inference' without direct evidence. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting these clinical associations without contesting the interpretation.

Both evaluate statistical methodology (C115-C118) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval describes the approach as 'methodologically sound' and 'well-justified' but notes missing reproducibility details. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the statistical section as 'very well written' with 'very sensible' approaches.

Both evaluate SMOTEENN for class imbalance (C114) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval calls it 'appropriate' for the 4.3% positive case rate, while peer reviewers include this in their praise of the statistical approach as 'sensible for the data in question.'

Both address WBC as top predictor (C61). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with mechanistic explanations from SHAP analysis. Peer reviewers rate laboratory findings as UNCERTAIN due to temporal concerns about whether features preceded PSE onset.

Both address brain region limited effects (C36) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes consistency with LASSO exclusion, while peer reviewers accept the statistical methodology determining feature importance without critique.

Both evaluate comorbidity findings (C37-C38) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval bases this on SHAP analysis visual evidence, while peer reviewers accept these clinical associations, noting the study 'may provide evidence of seizure prevention.'

OpenEval evaluates lipid profiles and coagulation parameters (C64-C72) as SUPPORTED with citations to prior literature and SHAP analysis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific biochemical predictors.

OpenEval evaluates uric acid's dual role and liver enzymes (C73-C82) as SUPPORTED, noting nuanced interpretation with plausible mechanisms. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific metabolic predictors.

OpenEval evaluates cardiac enzyme findings (C83-C89) as SUPPORTED, appropriately citing literature and acknowledging mechanistic uncertainty. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these cardiac biomarkers.

Minimal overlap on C25 (risk factors). OpenEval rates risk factor claims as UNCERTAIN due to missing effect sizes and multiple testing concerns. Peer reviewers' UNCERTAIN rating focuses on temporal ambiguity of laboratory features rather than statistical reporting issues.
